strengths: The paper presents a relevant and technically plausible Algorithms/General contribution: coordinate-free GUI grounding by directly supervising intrinsic MLLM attention, using an anchor token to avoid aggregating every instruction token and visual-sink tokens to weight attention heads.

The empirical results are strong. GUI-AIMA-3B reaches 45.2% on ScreenSpot-Pro without zoom-in and 58.6% with zoom-in, while remaining competitive on ScreenSpot-v2 (90.8%) and OSWorld-G (56.9% without zoom-in, 62.2% with it). The particularly large gains on difficult icon targets are valuable.

Table 4 provides a reasonably controlled 45k-sample comparison against GUI-Actor and vanilla attention grounding. It separately studies the anchor-based formulation, alternative head-weighting rules, visual-sink-token selection, and weighted patch labels; the complete formulation improves ScreenSpot-Pro from 35.99% for GUI-Actor to 43.39%.

The method is parameter-efficient in architecture: it does not introduce a separate grounding head or require GUI-Actor's warm-up stage. Training on approximately 85k distinct screenshots is also encouraging, though the paper actually uses 259k instruction instances.
The paper is generally clear, mathematically organized, and supported by useful visualizations and an analysis of the crop-and-zoom inference stage.
weaknesses: The headline 58.6% ScreenSpot-Pro result depends on a second inference pass with cropping and zooming, whereas competing entries in Table 1 apparently use ordinary inference. This is useful test-time scaling, but it is not a strictly controlled comparison. The corresponding one-pass result is 45.2%, and equivalent zoom-in results for the strongest baselines are not provided.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The project-page field is empty, and important details are missing, including the precise conversion from patch scores to click coordinates, image resizing/tokenization settings, crop handling near boundaries and coordinate remapping, optimizer and scheduler choices, initialization of all new tokens, and inference prompts. Sampling the "first" examples from several datasets also leaves potential ordering bias.

The claimed efficiency is only partially demonstrated. There are no measurements of training wall time, inference latency, memory, or attention-materialization cost. Extracting and supervising attention across every layer and head may be expensive or incompatible with common optimized-attention implementations. Counting 85k screenshots also obscures that training uses 259k instruction instances.

The central visual-sink interpretation is weakly validated. Figure 5 contains only five examples and frequently identifies the end-of-message token, while the paper does not quantitatively establish that the selected token or highly weighted heads have the claimed semantic function. The gain over uniform head weighting is modest on the controlled ablation: +0.62 points on ScreenSpot-v2 and +1.90 on ScreenSpot-Pro.

Several broader claims exceed the evidence. The assertion that direct supervision of ordinary query-token attention harms general capabilities is not tested on captioning or general multimodal benchmarks, and generalization is evaluated with only one 3B backbone. There are also no multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for relatively small ablation differences.

Most main-table baseline values are copied from original papers, potentially involving different data, preprocessing, or inference budgets. A full-data, same-backbone controlled comparison against GUI-Actor, vanilla attention grounding, and a standard coordinate-generation baseline would make the scientific case substantially stronger.

The overlap- and center-aware label construction is explicitly adapted from GUI-G2, so it should not be framed as a major original component. Overall originality is moderate: the main novelty is a useful combination of an anchor token and a heuristic attention-head weighting rule building on prior attention-based grounding.

Evaluation is limited to offline point-grounding accuracy. No end-to-end GUI-agent results, failure taxonomy, robustness analysis, or assessment of whether attention-derived clicks improve actual task completion is provided. The paper also lacks a meaningful limitations discussion covering these issues.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: efficient grounding of natural-language instructions in complex GUI screenshots.

The coordinate-free formulation is coherent, combining a learnable anchor token, intrinsic self-attention maps, and overlap- and center-aware patch supervision without adding a separate grounding head.

Evaluation covers three relevant benchmarks—ScreenSpot-v2, ScreenSpot-Pro, and OSWorld-G—and reports particularly strong ScreenSpot-Pro results. The two-step variant reaches 58.6%, while the base 3B model is competitive with substantially larger models.

The controlled 45k-sample study compares against vanilla attention grounding and GUI-Actor, and it separately investigates anchor-based aggregation, head weighting, visual-sink token selection, label weighting, and zoom-in inference.

The method appears practically useful for high-resolution interfaces: the crop-and-zoom stage substantially improves localization and Table 5 explicitly reports both corrected and degraded predictions.
weaknesses: The central technical novelty is fairly incremental. The method combines attention-based grounding, a special aggregation token, and Gaussian-style patch labeling drawn from prior work; the proposed visual-sink head weighting contributes only 1.90 points over uniform weighting on ScreenSpot-Pro in the controlled ablation.

The claimed efficiency is insufficiently demonstrated. Training still updates all parameters of a 3B model and seemingly requires materializing attention maps and hidden states across all layers, yet the paper reports no training time, inference latency, peak memory, FLOPs, or comparison under matched hardware. The two-step version also doubles inference passes, although it produces the headline 58.6% result.

Most headline baseline numbers are copied from original papers rather than reproduced under matched preprocessing, resolution, prompts, and inference budgets. These factors are especially consequential for GUI grounding, weakening the state-of-the-art and efficiency comparisons.

The empirical gains outside ScreenSpot-Pro are modest or mixed. On ScreenSpot-v2, the base model improves over GUI-Actor-3B by only 0.4 points and remains below several 7B systems. On OSWorld-G, even the two-step result of 62.2% remains below the reported 64.2% of UI-TARS-1.5-7B.

There are no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance analyses. Several claimed gains are small enough that run-to-run variation could affect the conclusions, and the ablations appear to select choices such as top-k and labeling directly using the reported benchmark test sets rather than a separate validation set.

The justification for visual-sink query tokens is weak. Figure 5 contains only five apparently selected examples and no aggregate quantitative analysis showing that hidden-state similarity reliably identifies semantically relevant tokens or attention heads.

Important claims are not tested: the paper asserts that supervising ordinary query-token attention harms general capabilities and that GUI-AIMA preserves pretrained capabilities, but it provides no captioning, VQA, or other general-capability evaluation. Generality is also evaluated only with one 3B backbone.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The project-page field is blank, and essential details are missing, including optimizer and schedule, preprocessing and token resolution, prompts, checkpoint selection, random seeds, precise crop/remapping and boundary handling, and whether gradients flow through the attention-head weights and top-k selection.

The training-data description does not document deduplication or overlap checks between the assembled datasets and evaluation benchmarks. Reporting 85k screenshots while training on 259k instruction instances also makes the data-efficiency framing potentially misleading relative to baselines counted in GUI elements.

The qualitative appendix presents only a handful of successful cases and no systematic failure analysis. Limitations involving small targets, crop-induced regressions, multi-region instructions, computational overhead, and reliance on benchmark bounding-box conventions are not meaningfully discussed.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution because no contribution type is explicitly declared. The paper presents a coherent and practically useful approach to GUI grounding: a learnable anchor token converts grounding into intrinsic attention-map prediction without adding a task-specific grounding module.

The experimental results are strong across three relevant benchmarks. The 3B model reaches 45.2% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 56.9% on OSWorld-G in one-pass inference, while the zoom-in variant reaches 58.6% and 62.2%, respectively, comparing favorably with similarly sized and several larger models.

The paper provides informative controlled ablations on a fixed 45k-example subset. These separately examine the anchor-based simplification, visual-sink token selection, head weighting, soft weighting, and overlap/center-aware patch labels. The convergence comparison also supports the claimed optimization advantage over vanilla attention grounding and GUI-Actor.

Training with approximately 85k screenshots and 259k instructions is relatively data-efficient. The approach is also architecturally economical, and the optional crop-and-zoom stage produces substantial improvements without additional training.
The method is motivated clearly, related closely to prior coordinate-free grounding work, and evaluated on both conventional and challenging high-resolution professional interfaces.
weaknesses: The strongest reported numbers depend on a second model pass with crop-and-zoom, but competing methods are not given the same refinement or matched test-time compute. Consequently, the comparison does not establish whether the large gains arise specifically from GUI-AIMA or from a generally applicable inference procedure. The one-pass advantage over GUI-Actor is considerably smaller on some benchmarks.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript lacks sufficiently precise prompts and output decoding details, image-resolution/tokenization settings, crop-boundary behavior, optimizer and schedule details, random seeds, and a substantive description of baseline implementations. The project-page field is also blank in the supplied manuscript.

Results are reported from apparently single runs without uncertainty estimates. Several ablation differences are small—for example, weighted labels and some visual-sink choices—so their robustness cannot be determined.

The interpretation of visual-sink query tokens and “semantic heads” is only weakly validated. Appendix A shows a small qualitative analysis in which the selected high-correlation token is often a special end token; this does not establish the proposed semantic mechanism or causal explanation. Stronger layer/head analyses or interventions would support the claim.

Efficiency claims focus primarily on training-data and convergence advantages, but no wall-clock training cost, inference latency, memory usage, or FLOPs are reported. This is especially important because aggregating attention across layers and heads can be expensive and zoom-in roughly adds another inference pass.

The evaluation is limited to offline point-in-box grounding. There is no end-to-end computer-use evaluation, robustness analysis, or failure breakdown beyond spatial offsets, so the practical impact on multi-step GUI agents remains uncertain.

strengths: The paper presents a relevant and reasonably original Algorithms/General contribution: direct supervision of an MLLM's intrinsic attention for coordinate-free GUI grounding. The anchor-token formulation is simple, avoids a separate grounding head, and is technically plausible.

The empirical coverage is broad, spanning ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, and MMBench-GUI-L2. GUI-AIMA-3B is particularly strong on high-resolution desktop grounding, reaching 61.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 68.1% on OSWorld-G with zoom-in.

The ablations are generally useful. The 45k-sample study separately examines anchored aggregation, alternative head-weighting rules, visual-sink token selection, and weighted patch labels; the larger-data appendix broadly corroborates the advantage over GUI-Actor and vanilla attention grounding.

The method has practical efficiency merits: it requires no separate warm-up stage, reports approximately 192 versus 260 A100 GPU-hours for GUI-Actor, and adds only modest single-pass inference overhead. The optional crop-and-zoom procedure is intuitive and yields substantial gains on dense interfaces.

The manuscript is organized clearly, relates the method to TAG and GUI-Actor, reports both lite and full-data variants, and explicitly identifies UI-Vision as in-domain rather than presenting it as an out-of-domain result.
weaknesses: Important implementation details needed for reproducibility are missing. The paper never precisely specifies how the final click coordinate is decoded from the patch distribution, how the attention and label vectors are normalized, how the attention loss is weighted against the retained next-token loss, or how boundary cases are handled during crop-and-zoom. Optimization and scheduling details are also sparse, and the project-page link is blank.

The headline data-efficiency and state-of-the-art comparisons are not fully controlled. Baselines use different datasets, backbones, training objectives, and inference budgets; many numbers are copied from prior papers. The strongest ScreenSpot-Pro and OSWorld-G results use a second model pass, while most compared systems use one pass, and UI-Vision is explicitly in-domain. The controlled same-data ablations are more persuasive than the broad ranking claims.

The motivation for selecting the 'visual-sink' token remains heuristic. Summed hidden-state similarity to all visual patches need not identify the instruction's target, and frequent selected tokens such as articles, punctuation, and newlines make the semantic interpretation unclear. Figure 7 offers only a small qualitative comparison to the learned anchor, without aggregate statistics or a stronger token-selection baseline.

Several reporting inconsistencies weaken confidence: the lite training set is variously described as 259k, 254k, and an '85k training set'; the added desktop subset is described as both 250k and 200k; and OSWorld-G versus OSWorld-G-Refine naming is inconsistent. In Table 6, the relationship among the original 306 offset errors, 215 corrected cases, 33 lost cases, and 147 remaining categorized errors is not adequately explained.

No run-to-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. This matters because some component gains are only about 1–2 percentage points, and hyperparameters such as top-1 token selection and the zoom factor appear selected using benchmark performance.

The demonstrated scope is single-region, single-click grounding rather than complete GUI-agent operation. Multi-target instructions, sequential interaction, robustness to adversarial or rapidly changing interfaces, and preservation of the backbone's general capabilities after full-parameter fine-tuning are not evaluated. Overall, the contribution is promising and empirically strong enough for a slight acceptance preference, but the incomplete specification and comparison caveats prevent a stronger score.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent Algorithms/General contribution: an anchor token aggregates query context, visual-sink tokens determine attention-head weights, and patch-wise supervision avoids textual coordinate generation. The approach introduces no separate grounding head and adds only modest measured inference overhead.

Evaluation is unusually broad, covering ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, MMBench-GUI-L2, and ScreenSpot-v1, with comparisons against general-purpose, supervised, and reinforcement-trained GUI models.
The reported 3B-model results are strong, especially 61.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 68.1% on OSWorld-G with zoom-in. The method also improves substantially over its Qwen2.5-VL-3B backbone.

The ablations compare vanilla attention grounding, anchor-based aggregation, several head-weighting choices, weighted patch labels, stop-gradient behavior, and GUI-Actor. Efficiency measurements and head-pruning analysis provide additional useful evidence.
weaknesses: The scientific case does not adequately separate the core attention method from extra data and test-time computation. The largest headline results use two forward passes with crop-and-zoom, while most baselines are reported under their original one-pass settings. The full model also adds 250k desktop-focused examples; consequently, its improvements cannot be attributed cleanly to the proposed attention formulation.

The central 'visual-sink' justification is weak. Equation (4) sums cosine similarity over every visual patch, favoring tokens associated with global visual statistics rather than target semantics. Figure 4 indeed selects articles, punctuation, and newline tokens most often. Figure 7 then shows similarity to the learned anchor, which is circular evidence and does not establish that these tokens identify grounding-relevant heads. The direct gain over uniform head weighting is only 1.90 points on ScreenSpot-Pro in the 45k ablation.

The paper reports no multiple-seed results, confidence intervals, or significance analysis. This is important because several component gains are small—1.90 points for head weighting and 1.26 points for weighted labeling—and may be sensitive to training or evaluation variation.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The project-page field is empty, and the manuscript does not fully specify the combined loss and its weighting, the exact conversion from patch attention to a click coordinate, crop handling near image boundaries, image resizing, or all relevant training details. There are also inconsistent data counts: 259k versus 254k samples, and 250k versus 200k added desktop instructions.

The claimed data efficiency is not established through controlled scaling experiments. Comparisons use different datasets, backbones, objectives, training stages, and inference procedures; counting examples alone does not demonstrate sample efficiency. The method still fully fine-tunes all 3B parameters for approximately 192 A100 GPU-hours.

Calling the method 'coordinate-free' is overstated: supervision is constructed from coordinate-defined bounding boxes, and deployment must ultimately recover a click coordinate from a patch distribution. The actual contribution is better described as avoiding coordinate-token generation.

UI-Vision is explicitly in-domain, and the manuscript gives no systematic audit of overlap or near-duplication between its heterogeneous training sources and the other evaluation benchmarks. The qualitative appendix shows only successful cases and provides no failure analysis, robustness tests, or evaluation under ambiguous/multi-target instructions.

Overall, the method is promising and the empirical results are competitive, but the novelty over existing attention-based grounding is incremental and the evidence does not yet convincingly validate the proposed mechanism or the stronger efficiency claims. These concerns slightly outweigh the merits.

strengths: The paper presents a technically plausible and useful Algorithms/General contribution: an anchor token aggregates instruction context, while visual-sink tokens provide adaptive attention-head weighting for coordinate-free GUI grounding. This is a coherent extension beyond vanilla attention aggregation and avoids a separate grounding head.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, MMBench-GUI-L2, and ScreenSpot-v1. GUI-AIMA-3B is consistently competitive with or better than similarly sized systems, with particularly strong results on high-resolution desktop grounding.

The paper provides informative component ablations at two training scales. The results support the anchor formulation, visual-sink-based head weighting, weighted patch labels, and zoom-in inference. Head-pruning experiments further corroborate that the learned weighting identifies grounding-relevant heads.

The two-step crop-and-zoom procedure is simple and practically effective. The corrected-versus-lost analysis is more revealing than reporting aggregate accuracy alone, and the substantial ScreenSpot-Pro gains demonstrate the value of patch-level predictions.

Efficiency is a meaningful advantage: the method introduces no separate grounding network or warm-up stage, reports lower training cost than GUI-Actor, and adds only modest overhead for attention extraction during one-pass inference.

The presentation is generally clear, with intuitive diagrams, extensive quantitative tables, and qualitative attention visualizations. Relevant coordinate-based and coordinate-free literature is discussed and appropriately positioned.
weaknesses: Important training details are underspecified. The paper states that next-token prediction is retained in addition to the attention KL loss, but never clearly defines the complete objective, its loss weights, or the exact textual target. It also does not fully specify how the final attention distribution is decoded into a click coordinate. These omissions materially hinder reproduction.

The data-efficiency comparison is not fully controlled. Competing systems use different datasets, backbones, training stages, and supervision, while GUI-AIMA-3B incorporates 250k GroundCUA examples and is explicitly in-domain on UI-Vision. Claims based mainly on nominal sample counts should therefore be qualified.

There are inconsistencies in the data description: the added desktop subset is described as 250k examples in the setup but as 200k in the main-results discussion, and the manuscript alternates between GroundCUA and GroundNext terminology. The project-page field is also blank, leaving no code or configuration resource for verification.

No results over multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. This matters for several modest gains, such as the roughly 1–2 point improvements attributed to visual-sink weighting and weighted patch labeling.

The strongest high-resolution results use two forward passes, but the efficiency table reports only ordinary per-iteration timing and does not quantify end-to-end latency or memory for zoom-in inference. Comparisons with single-pass baselines therefore mix accuracy and compute budgets despite the notation in the tables.

The novelty is moderate rather than fundamental: the method combines prior attention-based grounding, a learned special-token aggregator, adaptive head weighting, an existing Gaussian-style labeling idea, and crop-and-rerun inference. The strong execution and evidence make this acceptable, but the paper occasionally overstates the conceptual departure.

The evaluation is limited to static single-target grounding. There is no end-to-end computer-use evaluation, robustness analysis for ambiguous instructions or multiple valid targets, or substantive discussion of failure cases and deployment risks associated with erroneous GUI actions.
